column1: # /usr/share/w/defaults/session-apps.tsv — relaunch overrides for `w-session`.
# W's own defaults. Do NOT edit: every update overwrites this file wholesale.
# Personal entries belong in ~/.config/w/session-apps.tsv, which the update
# never touches; both files are read, and the user's file wins on a tie.
# WHAT THIS IS FOR
# `w-session save` recovers each window's relaunch command from
# /proc/<pid>/cmdline, which is right for the overwhelming majority of programs:
# the argv a window's process was started with is exactly what reopens it, down
# to the document it has open. This table is the escape hatch for the cases
# where it is not:
#   • the cmdline is meaningless — the window belongs to a D-Bus-activated
#     service, a portal, or a wrapper that has already exec'd away;
#   • the cmdline is correct but WRONG FOR W — see the terminals below.
# Format: <initialClass regex>\t<command>[\t<flag>...]
#   The regex is anchored (`foot` matches `foot`, not `footclient`) and matched
#   against the window's `initialClass`, never its live class: a program that
#   renames itself at runtime must still be recognisable a reboot later.
#   The command is run through `sh -c` in the window's saved working directory,
#   so a relative path in it means what it meant when the window was open.
#   First match wins; a command of `-` means "never relaunch this class", and
#   `=` means "the recorded command line is fine" — a row that only sets flags.
#   '#' and blank lines are ignored.
# Flags:
#   own-session   The program keeps its own session and ONE launch brings back
#                 every window it had. `w-session` therefore launches it once
#                 for all of its saved windows, waits for them, and puts each
#                 back where a window with the same title was. Launching it once
#                 per window would not open the saved windows — the second
#                 launch is a remote command to the running instance and opens
#                 a blank one.
# Terminals resolve to `w-term`, not to the binary they happened to be.
# This is the one entry that is not about a broken cmdline. `w-term` is W's
# single terminal entry point: it maps to whichever terminal the machine is
# configured for (/etc/w/terminal.conf) and launches it the systemd/D-Bus-
# correct way. Recording `ghostty` verbatim would pin the restored session to
# the terminal that was active the day it was saved — switch terminals and every
# saved window reopens the old one, or fails to reopen at all once it is
# uninstalled. The working directory, which is the part that actually carries
# your work (a shell in a repo, yazi, nvim), is preserved either way.
com\.mitchellh\.ghostty
foot
# Firefox restores its own windows and tabs (Settings → Home and startup → "Open
# previous windows and tabs"). Closing its windows one by one at logout marks
# them as a series to reopen, and `w-session close` finishes that series for it
# once it has quit (Firefox's own pass stops at any older closed window). See
# w-session.md.
firefox
